# Stickney Crater on Phobos

When a massive space rock slammed into Mars's tiny moon Phobos, it carved out a crater so enormous—9 kilometers wide—that it nearly destroyed the entire moon, which is only twice as large. Named after mathematician Chloe Stickney Hall (wife of the astronomer who discovered both Martian moons in 1877), this giant impact scar reveals mysterious clues about the moon's violent past, including strange grooves and freshly exposed bluish rocks, all captured in stunning detail by NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter in 2008.
